title: Block distracting websites during study hours
devices: Firefox, Chrome or Edge on Windows, Mac, Linux or Chromebook. Also Firefox for Android.
summary: Set up a free, open-source browser extension that blocks YouTube, social media or any site you choose — only during the hours you are meant to be studying.
why: Nearly one in three students say digital devices distract them in class (OECD, PISA 2022), and it can take up to 20 minutes to refocus after a distraction (UNESCO GEM Report 2023). Blocking the few sites that pull you away is easier than relying on willpower.
screenshotNote: Screenshots were taken on 11 November 2026 in a fresh browser profile with no accounts signed in. The options-page images show LeechBlock NG version 1.8's own options page with example settings typed in.

steps.title: Install LeechBlock NG from your browser's add-on store
steps.body: Open the official listing for your browser — Firefox Add-ons, the Chrome Web Store or Edge Add-ons (links below) — and choose Add to Firefox / Add to Chrome / Get. It is free, with no account and no paid version.

image.alt: The Firefox Add-ons page for LeechBlock NG by James Anderson. It shows a short description, a Recommended badge, a 4.8 star rating from 2,064 reviews, 113,322 users, and a button to get the extension.
image.caption: The official Firefox Add-ons listing. Check the developer name (James Anderson) so you install the real extension.

steps.title: Open the LeechBlock options page
steps.body: Click the LeechBlock shield icon in your toolbar and choose Options. In Chrome or Edge the icon may be hidden: click the puzzle-piece Extensions button first, then pin LeechBlock so it stays visible.

steps.title: Name your block set and list the sites
steps.body: In the What to Block section, type a name such as "Study hours". Then enter the sites that distract you most, one per line — for example youtube.com, instagram.com, tiktok.com and reddit.com. Keep the list short: three to five sites is enough to start.

image.alt: LeechBlock's What to Block section. The block set name box contains 'Study hours' and the site list contains youtube.com, instagram.com, tiktok.com and reddit.com, one per line.
image.caption: Example block set. Use the + prefix to allow an exception, for example a single lecture playlist.

steps.title: Choose when the block applies
steps.body: In When to Block, enter your study periods as 24-hour times, e.g. 0900-1230,1330-1700. If you would rather allow a little browsing, also set a time limit such as 10 minutes in every hour. Tick the days you study — for example Monday to Friday.

image.alt: LeechBlock's When to Block section with time periods 0900-1230,1330-1700, a limit of 10 minutes in every hour, the rule 'within time periods OR after time limit', and Monday to Friday ticked.
image.caption: Blocks apply 9:00–12:30 and 13:30–17:00 on weekdays, or once you have used 10 minutes in an hour.

steps.tip: Not sure about the OR / AND setting? OR blocks during your study periods and also after the time limit. AND only blocks once the limit is used up inside a study period.

steps.title: Save, then test it
steps.body: Press Save Options (at the bottom of the page). Now open one of your blocked sites during a study period: you should see LeechBlock's blocked page instead. If the site still loads, check that today's day is ticked and the times use the 24-hour format.

image.alt: The Save Options and Save Options & Close buttons at the bottom of the LeechBlock options page.
image.caption: Settings only take effect after you save.

steps.title: Optional: make it harder to switch off
steps.body: If you keep undoing your own blocks, open the General tab and use Access Control to require a password or a long random code before the options can be changed. You can also tick "Prevent access to options for this block set at times when these sites are blocked" in the block set's advanced options.

troubleshooting.a: Make sure you pressed Save Options, the current day is ticked, and the time periods are written like 0900-1700 (no colons). Private/incognito windows need the extension allowed there too.

troubleshooting.q: I need one YouTube video for class.
troubleshooting.a: Add an exception line starting with +, for example +youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID, or temporarily use a different block set.

troubleshooting.q: Does it work on my phone?
troubleshooting.a: Only in Firefox for Android. For phone apps use your phone's built-in app timers (see the phone wind-down guide).

title: A 15-minute privacy and account check-up
tool: Have I Been Pwned, Bitwarden and Privacy Badger
devices: Any web browser. Bitwarden also has phone and desktop apps; Privacy Badger works in Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Brave and Safari on Mac.
summary: Check whether your email has appeared in a data breach, start using a different strong password for every account, and block hidden trackers — all with free tools.
why: Over half of UK 13–17-year-olds have avoided apps that asked for personal information they weren't comfortable sharing, yet 12% always share it anyway (Ofcom, 2025). A few basic habits protect your accounts and reduce how much of your browsing is tracked.
screenshotNote: Screenshots were taken on 11 November 2026 in a fresh browser profile with no accounts signed in. We did not screenshot Have I Been Pwned because its bot check blocks automated browsers — the steps below describe what you will see.

steps.title: Check your email on Have I Been Pwned
steps.body: Go to haveibeenpwned.com, type your email address and press Check. The site is free for personal checks and says it does not store what you search for. If your address appears in a breach, note which sites are listed — you will change those passwords first in step 3. Then use Notify Me to get a free email if your address shows up in a future breach.
steps.tip: "Good news — no pwnage found" only means your address is not in the breaches HIBP knows about. It does not prove your accounts are safe.

steps.title: Create a free Bitwarden account and a strong master password
steps.body: Download Bitwarden for your phone, computer or browser from bitwarden.com/download and create a free account. The free plan covers unlimited passwords on unlimited devices. Choose a master password you can remember but nobody could guess — a passphrase of four or more random words works well. Bitwarden cannot recover it for you, so write it down and keep it somewhere safe at home.

image.alt: Bitwarden's password generator page with the headline 'Create seriously strong passwords', buttons to get started or try the free password generator, and an image of the generator showing a 14-character random password.
image.caption: Bitwarden's free generator. Inside the app, the same generator is one tap away when you save a new login.

steps.title: Replace your most important passwords first
steps.body: Start with your email account (it can reset every other password), then any account flagged in step 1, then school and banking. For each one: log in, open account or security settings, change the password, and let Bitwarden generate and save a new one. You do not have to do every account today — add others as you log in to them.

steps.title: Turn on two-step verification for your email
steps.body: In your email account's security settings, turn on two-step verification (also called 2FA or MFA). After your password you will also confirm a code or prompt on your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough. The short CISA video on our Videos page shows why it matters.

steps.title: Install Privacy Badger to block hidden trackers
steps.body: Add Privacy Badger from your browser's add-on store (links below). It is free and open source from the nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). There is nothing to set up: it learns to block trackers as you browse. Click the badger icon on any site to see what it has blocked, and move a slider to green if a site stops working.

image.alt: The Firefox Add-ons page for Privacy Badger by EFF Technologists, with a description of how it automatically learns to block invisible trackers and a button to get the extension.
image.caption: The official listing. Check that it is published by EFF Technologists.

troubleshooting.q: I forgot my Bitwarden master password.
troubleshooting.a: Bitwarden cannot see or reset it because your vault is end-to-end encrypted. That is why step 2 asks you to write it down and keep it safe offline.

troubleshooting.q: A website broke after installing Privacy Badger.
troubleshooting.a: Click the badger icon and use "Disable for this site", or move the slider for the broken item to yellow or green.
No. Premium (US$19.80/year, checked 11 November 2026) adds extras such as built-in 2FA codes and vault health reports, but storing and generating passwords is free.

title: Phone wind-down: app timers, bedtime mode and quieter notifications
tool: Google Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Apple Screen Time & Focus (iPhone)
devices: Android phones with Digital Wellbeing (most recent phones) or iPhone. Menu names can differ slightly by phone maker and software version.
summary: Use the tools already on your phone to set a daily limit for your most-used app, switch to a calmer screen at bedtime, and bundle non-urgent notifications.
why: Teens received a median of 237 notifications a day in one study, and 59% used their phone between midnight and 5 a.m. on school nights (Common Sense Media, 2023). In a 3-week experiment, students who limited social media to 10 minutes per app per day reported less loneliness and depression (Hunt et al., 2018).
screenshotNote: The phone pictures in this guide are illustrations drawn for this hub, not screenshots, because we did not want to capture a real phone's personal notifications or app list. Menu wording was checked against Google's and Apple's official help pages on 11 November 2026.

steps.title: Set an app timer for your most-used app
steps.body: Open Settings › Digital Wellbeing (on some phones "Digital Wellbeing & parental controls") › App timers. Next to the app you lose the most time to, tap Set timer, choose a daily amount such as 30 minutes, and tap OK. When time runs out the app closes and its icon dims until midnight.

image.alt: Illustration of Android's App timers screen with a list of apps and a 30-minute timer being set for a video app.
image.caption: Illustration, not a real screenshot. Wording from Google's Digital Wellbeing help page.

steps.title: Schedule Bedtime mode
steps.body: In Digital Wellbeing tap Bedtime mode › Bedtime routine. Choose Use a schedule and set your sleep start and end times and days, or choose Turn on while charging. Under Customize › Screen options at bedtime, turn on Grayscale and Keep the screen dark so late-night scrolling feels less tempting.

image.alt: Illustration of Android's Bedtime mode screen with 'Use a schedule' selected from 22:30 to 07:00 on school nights and Grayscale switched on.
image.caption: Illustration, not a real screenshot. Wording from Google's Digital Wellbeing help page.

steps.title: Use Focus mode for homework
steps.body: In Digital Wellbeing tap Focus mode, tick the apps that distract you, then choose Set a schedule (for example weekdays 16:00–18:00) or Turn on now. While it is on, those apps are paused and their notifications are held back. Take a break unpauses them for a short time if you really need one.

steps.title: Turn on Screen Time and set a daily allowance
steps.body: Open Settings › Screen Time and turn it on. On iOS 27 tap Time Allowances, choose a category such as Social Media, and drag the slider to your daily limit. On iOS 26 or earlier the same feature is called App Limits (Settings › Screen Time › App Limits › Add Limit).

image.alt: Illustration of iPhone's Screen Time Time Allowances screen with a Social Media category set to 45 minutes a day.
image.caption: Illustration, not a real screenshot. Wording from Apple's iPhone User Guide for iOS 27.

steps.tip: By default you can choose to ignore a limit once it is reached. To make limits stick, set a Screen Time passcode — or ask a friend or parent to set it.

steps.title: Set a sleep schedule and Sleep Focus
steps.body: Open the Health app › Browse › Sleep › Get Started and set your sleep schedule. You can add a wind-down period of 15 minutes to 3 hours before bedtime. Then in Settings › Focus › Sleep choose which people and apps may still reach you — Sleep Focus starts at the beginning of your wind-down.

image.alt: Illustration of iPhone's Sleep Focus settings showing a wind-down starting 45 minutes before a 22:30 bedtime, with only family allowed to notify.
image.caption: Illustration, not a real screenshot. Wording from Apple's iPhone User Guide.

steps.title: Bundle non-urgent notifications
steps.body: Go to Settings › Notifications › Scheduled Summary, turn it on, pick one or two times a day (for example 13:00 and 18:00), then choose which apps to include. Their notifications arrive together at those times instead of interrupting you all day.

troubleshooting.a: Search Settings for "Digital Wellbeing" or "Screen time". Google says it is available on some phones, and some brands use their own name for it.

troubleshooting.q: My iPhone says Downtime, not Screen Time Schedule.
troubleshooting.a: That is the older name used on iOS 26 and earlier. Settings › Screen Time › Downtime does the same job.

troubleshooting.q: I keep ignoring my own limits.
troubleshooting.a: Set a Screen Time passcode and turn on Block at Downtime (iPhone), or set an App limits PIN (Android). Research suggests limits work better when they are harder to switch off, but are also more frustrating — start with a limit you can live with.
